A DOZEN monkeys had a "durian buffet" at the back of a lorry transporting the fruits
from Kuala Lumpur back to Bentong, Pahang. The incident happened on Friday
afternoon along the Karak Highway just past the toll plaza when lorry driver Zou Sheng
Zhe stopped to have a break. "I was 10 minutes into a nap when I was woken up by a
lorry honking next to mine. I looked into the rear-view mirror and saw more than 10
monkeys at the back of my lorry feasting on my durians," Zou said. He admitted that he .APA "IAAPRIC1/1
was fearful of being attacked and therefore did not try to chase them away. He added
that he would often take a nap along the Karak Highway whenever he was delivering
durians to and from the capital. However, he admitted that this was his first-time
encountering monkeys stealing his fruits.
Adapted from The Star

durians.
KOTA BARU: Para-athlete gold medalist Nurul Ain Natasha Marzuki is not only good on
the track. The girl, who was born without a right arm, spent five hours a day studying for
her Sijil Tinggi Persekolahan Malaysia (STPM) examination and managed to achieve a
3.42 cumulative grade point average (CGPA). Nurul Ain Natasha, 20, from SMK
Pengkalan Chepa here, told she wants to become a teacher, and she intended to
pursue her studies at Universiti Pendidikan Sultan Idris as well as representing
Malaysia at the SEA Games. She said her disability was not an obstacle to her in her
studies or daily life. "Ihave to rely only on my left hand almost all the time, for writing,
eating and so on, but it does not weaken my spirit," told Nurul Ain.
Adapted from BERNAMA

A She was concerned that her disability would prevent her from being excel in
studies and sports.
B She was so hardworking and motivated to get good result in STPM,
despite of her disability.
C She wanted to become a teacher at SMK Pengkalan Chepa after finishing her
studies at Universiti Pendidikan Sultan Idris.

KUALA LUMPUR: Selangor Red Giants (SRG) ended Malaysia's seven-year drought in
international esports by defeating the Philippines' AP Bren Sport 4-2 in the Mobile
Legends: Bang Bang (MLBB) Mid Season Cup (MSC) 2024 last night. In the grand final
held in Riyadh, SRG seemed to give no chance to AP Bren, dominating the game and
continuing their momentum to defeat the opponents, thus securing the MSC
championship for the first time. SRG's member Muhammad Haqqullah Ahmad Shahrul,
also known as Sekyss, was named the most valuable player (MVP) of the competition.
The victory saw SRG taking home the trophy and a cash prize of US$1mil (RM4.7mil).
Adapted from The Star
4 Which of the following statements is true?
A AP Bren Sport was one of the finalists in the competition.
B Sekyss won US$1mil after becoming the MVP of the competition.
C SRG won the MSC championship for the first time seven years ago.
Humanoid Robot - Torobo
In Japan, a DIY-helper robot has now been demonstrated, capable of sawing a plank of
wood and hammering in a nail. Called Torobo, this humanoid robot can interact with its
environment and nearby humans, and manipulate objects. The configuration of its arm
and waist joints enables it to perform tasks with a range of movement similar to that of a
human being. Automatic learning also enables it to master more complex movements, as
in this case for DIY work. This 1.60m- tall robot can now hammer in a nail on its own. It
can hold a hammer correctly, control its power and withstand the hammer's
instantaneous rebound force. It has also learned how to saw a plank of wood and clean a
table with a cloth.
Adapted from The Star

5 Which of the following statement is true about Torobo, a humanoid robot?
A Torobo is built to help people to interact with each other and also the
environment.
B Torobo can learn automatically so that it will be able to pick up more difficult
movements.
C Torobo knows how to hammer correctly, but it cannot withstand the hammer's
instantaneous rebound force.
GEORGE TOWN: It might be a little depressing for some Penangites taking evening
walks by the beach of late. Dozens of small dead fish are regularly washing up,
testament to the fact that the sweltering heat caused by the El Nino weather
phenomenon is killing weaker fish. Many Penangites have shared the ugly sight of rotten
spotted scat, small croakers, and juvenile catfish appearing along the beach. The spotted
scat is a macro feeder, dwelling in submerged rocks just off the seashore, while young
croakers and catfish hug close to the coastline and dare not venture into deeper waters
for fear of predators. "Because they live so close to the seashore, they are more at risk of
heatwaves," said Universiti Sains Malaysia's (USM) fish expert, Dr Khaironizam Md Zain.
Adapted from nst.com.my
6 Which of the following statements is true about the newspaper extract?
A The extreme hot weather kills the fish.
B Scat, croakers and catfish live far from the seashore.
C Penangites are feeling depressed over the hot weather.

While festivities bring communities together, we also witness a surge in food wastage
due to excessive preparation and purchasing habits. One way to address this is by
being mindful of our food consumption. Thus, efforts should be made to promote food
rescue initiatives, by redirecting surplus food to those in need rather than allowing it to
go to waste. Food and beverage (F&B) businesses also have an important role to play.
Numerous studies have found that many companies experience significant cost savings
over time by setting up waste reduction initiatives, which include minimising
overproduction and optimising inventory. One way that our government can help F&B
businesses is by providing grants or subsidies.
Adapted from nst.com.my
7 Which of the following statement about food wastage is not true?
A Waste reduction programmes can help F&B businesses to save costs.
B Government can help in this initiative by providing subsidies to everyone.
C Surplus food can be distributed to those in need to prevent it to go to waste.
The number of people with depression has doubled in the last four years. This raises the
question of why mental illness is on the rise. Mental health issues like depression have
been around since time immemorial, says counselling psychologist Prem Kumar
Shanmugam. The difference now is that we have become more aware of such issues
and have better tools to diagnose them. However, these issues may also be over-
diagnosed or even misdiagnosed, he says. For example, there is a huge difference
between depression and feeling sad. "Depression is a clinical diagnosis with symptoms
like inability to sleep, massive weight loss and constant crying for no reason. Sadness, on
the other hand, is just an emotion." Due to easy access to information on the Internet,
people can over-diagnose or misdiagnose themselves too.
Adapted from nst.com.my
8 From the extract above, we can conclude that
A the rise of mental illness is due to depression and sadness.
B information on the internet is effective to diagnose our mental state.
C many people are unsure they are either having depression or just feeling sad.

Looking back on my childhood, my fondest memory is of sitting in the
kitchen to watch my mother cook, we were then living in Ipoh, Malaya. There
was a depression going on after the Second World War, Dad was newly
demobilised and struggled to make a living with his small grocery shop. I was
then almost six years old. My parents, my sister and two brothers and | all lived
huddled together in a shabby wooden hut. Mum, who had lived a comfortable,
well-to-do life, had now to worry about our daily bread.
Times were so hard so my mother could only make us ordinary dishes,
such as vegetables with dried shrimp, fried steamed chicken with salted fish and
fried chicken slices with greens. But for me, sitting at that humble wooden table
with the whole family, and gobbling up the steamy rice and the simple food, each
mouthful tasted like ambrosia. Once in a while Mum cooked her favourite dish of
steamed chicken with taro, and that would be a big occasion indeed.
When I was eight, our whole family moved south to Singapore. Life didn't
improve much as all six of us were forced to huddle in a rented room at Kallang.
Living conditions were really difficult. Seven or eight families shared one big flat,
and people squabbled and bickered constantly. Mum would have none of it. line 17
She was a quiet person and had no appetite for gossip. She preferred to stick to
her family behind closed kitchen doors - and when she had to stir out of the
room she would go her own way, minding, her own business.
She was determined not to let the crowded conditions prevent her from
feeding her family properly. Cooking in the apartment was done not with
firewood, but coal. During the hardest times, when we couldn't afford the big
bags of fuel, Mum would take us by the hand and go to the coal shop to buy
small quantities of the black cake. Walking home with it loosely wrapped in old

paper, she would move slowly, restrained, as it seemed, by the shackles of our
hard life. Later, she would feed the coal into a small stove and fan a small flame
into a raging fire. She then cooked for the family amid the steaming heat.
I'm sure she had much to worry about though she did not share her fears
with us. Dad was working very hard at his construction business and was out
day and night. Quite often, Mum cooked the food, shared a quick meal with us
and kept our father's portion in a big bowl with a blue floral pattern, packed line 32
full and solid.
Home late in the evening, Dad was tired and hungry, his eyes bloodshot
and cheeks visibly sunken. The night was deep, and it was not possible to start
another fire to warm the food; so he would gulp down his cold dinner ravenously
under a dim light surrounded by Mum and us kids. Still, despite these hardships,
the whole room was warm with happiness. For Dad, the cold food must have
tasted delicious as it was made with love. During our first two years in
Singapore, life was a struggle, but slowly our fortunes improved. In 1960, when I
was ten years old, we moved into a new apartment at Kim Tian Road. We now
had a gas stove.
The road that Mum and Dad travelled was an arduous one. Now, sitting
on the verandah amidst the gorgeous flowers, they enjoy peace after those
difficult years. As for myself, 1 appreciate the comforts they have earned, but
even more still, remember the days of hardship when my mother lovingly
laboured over a small stove with little more than a few sticks of wood, a pot and
her imagination to feed us. We had little then, but the happiness my mother
radiated from her kitchen stove made us feel we had everything.
Adapted from : Reader's Digest January 2019

The Green Water Phenomenon in Kampung Kuala Hau
Kampung Kuala Hau, a village in Kelantan, has recently attracted attention due to an
unusual natural event: the local river has turned a striking green. This phenomenon,
which has gained significant interest after images and videos went viral on social media,
is not new to the villagers. 27
For about three years, residents of Kampung Kuala Hau have observed the river
changing colour to green during periods of heavy rain. According to the villagers, this
event is a common occurrence. The river in question is an upstream watercourse that,
under specific conditions mainly during intense and sustained rainfall transforms into a
greenish hue. 28
Despite the attention, the green water phenomenon is not considered alarming by the
local residents. They view it as a routine part of the flood season, having experienced
similar occurrences in past years. 29 [ This has led investigation teams to visit
the site.
Wan Aminordin Wan Kamaruddin, Director of the Department of Environment in
Kelantan, has initiated an investigation into the green water. 30 This testing is
crucial for understanding the composition of the water and determining whether any
pollutants or unusual substances are contributing to the green colour.
31 Algae can produce pigments that give water a green appearance,
especially when environmental conditions such as water temperature and nutrient levels
are favourable. The results of the chemical tests will provide clarity on whether algae or
other factors are responsible for the colour change.

This investigation highlights the importance of monitoring natural events and their
impacts on local ecosystems. While the green water has been a known event for the
villagers, the increased interest from outside the community emphasizes the need for
scientific analysis. 32
In summary, the green water phenomenon in Kampung Kuala Hau is a recurrent
event during the flood season. While it has recently gained wider attention, it remains a
familiar occurrence for the local residents. The ongoing investigation by environmental
authorities aims to understand the underlying causes of the water's colour and to assess
any potential environmental or health concerns. The results from the chemical analysis
will be crucial in providing a comprehensive understanding of this natural event.

the Department of Chemistry for analysis.

and animals.

or public health.

about the dramatic shift in colour.

WAYS TO IMPROVE SPORTS IN MALAYSIA
A - HAZIQ, 17 years old
Focussing in youth sports programs is key. By enhancing grassroots development,
we can identify and nurture talent from an early age. Improved training standards and
education at the youth level will create a strong foundation for future athletes, ensuring
long-term success and increasing Malaysia's competitiveness in international sports.
B - MARK, 15 years old
Improving coaching standards through specialized training programs is vital. Skilled
coaches bring better techniques and strategies, directly benefiting athletes' performance.
Ongoing professional development for coaches will ensure they stay current with global best
practices, leading to higher quality training and better outcomes for Malaysian sports.
C - FEEYA, 16 years old
Upgrading local sports facilities is essential for boosting participation and
performance. Modern,well-maintained venues will attract more athletes and can host
regional events. Increasing investments in these areas ensures a better training
environment, which is crucial for developing both recreational and competitive sports in
Malaysia.
D - RADJA, 18 years old
Enhancing sports visibility through media coverage can significantly boost interest
and participation. By highlighting local events and athletes, we can inspire more people to
engage in sports. Effective media campaigns also attract sponsorships and create role
models, helping to grow the sports culture in Malaysia.
E - HARIS, 17 years old
Fostering inclusivity in sports is crucial. Programs that encourage participation from
women and individuals with disabilities can broaden the talent pool and promote equality.
Making sports accessible to diverse groups enriches the sports community and ensures that
everyone has the opportunity to contribute and excel.
F - LEONA, 15 years old
Collaborating with international sports organizations can bring valuable insights and
expertise. These partnerships allow us to adopt global best practices and offer local athletes
international exposure. By integrating these practices, we can elevate Malaysia's sports
standards and better prepare our athletes for global competition.
